newsitem.title: LEBANON: Hizbollah says it not behind Katyusha attack.
newsitem.headline: Hizbollah says it not behind Katyusha attack.

text.p: Lebanon's pro-Iranian Hizbollah said on Friday it has not launched any Katyusha rockets into Israel after the Israeli army said rockets slammed into the country's northern region.
"We the Islamic Reistance deny firmly that we have launched any Katyusha rockets on Friday," a Hizbollah (Party of God) official, who declined to be named, told Reuters.
Officials of three radical Palestinian guerrilla factions in Lebanon contacted by Reuters also said they had not carried out any rocket attacks on northern Israel.

The Israeli army said Katyusha rockets slammed into the Western Galilee region of northern Israel earlier on Friday at about 8 pm (1800 gmt) from Qlaileh area of southern Lebanon. There were no reports of casualties or damage, it said.
The rocket attack was the first such assault against northern Israel since a U.S.-brokered understanding ended a 17-day Israeli blitz against Hizbollah guerrillas in April.

Hizbollah -- which followed a policy of firing Katyushas into Israel whenever Israeli shelling caused Lebanese civilian casualties -- has refrained from such attacks under the accord that bars the targetting of civilians areas by both sides.

Earlier on Friday, Hizbollah MP Mohammad Fneish said the group was "dissatisfied" with a statement by a five-nation ceasefire monitoring group -- set up under the ceasefire understandings -- which had held Israel responsible for the injury of six Lebanese civilians on Saturday.
"The statements issued by the (monitoring) committee do not compensate for anything and the Lebanese people can not bear this excess and recklessness with people's lives and belgonings," Fneish said.

The group comprising the United States, France, Israel, Lebanon and Syria, said it "deplored" by unanimity the injuries caused to the Lebanese civilians by Israeli shelling and the damage to houses in the two villages on December 7.
The Saturday shelling followed an attack by Moslem guerrillas that killed one Israeli soldier and wounded another.
It was the third time in succession the monitoring group has held Israel responsible for shelling a south Lebanon village.
In Israel, an army spokesman said the Katyusha attack was a blunt violation of the ceasefire understandings.
Some 200 people, mainly civilians, were killed in the 17 days of relentless Israeli air, land and sea bombardment in April aimed at crushing Hizbollah.
The ceasefire agreement does not bar guerrilla raids on Israeli forces occupying a border zone in south Lebanon, and gives both sides the right to self-defence.
Israel set up the 15-km (nine-miles)-deep south zone when it withdrew the bulk of its 1982 invasion force in 1985 to protect its northern settlements from guerrilla attacks.
